name: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data
title: Combining Qualitative and Quantitative Data
answer: Combining qualitative and quantitative data means bringing together non-numeric evidence such as interviews, field notes, documents, or open-ended survey responses with numeric measures, counts, or model outputs. In AI research this often involves pairing human interpretation of text, images, or behavior with metrics from experiments or system logs. The goal is to explain not just what happened but why, and to check findings across different kinds of evidence. This approach sits within mixed methods and is used when a single data type cannot capture a research question fully.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Combining qualitative and quantitative data means bringing together non-numeric evidence such as interviews, field notes, documents, or open-ended survey responses with numeric measures, counts, or model outputs. In AI research this often involves pairing human interpretation of text, images, or behavior with metrics from experiments or system logs. The goal is to explain not just what happened but why, and to check findings across different kinds of evidence. This approach sits within mixed methods and is used when a single data type cannot capture a research question fully.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work usually runs on standard research computing rather than specialized AI hardware. Qualitative data may be stored in documents, spreadsheets, or qualitative data analysis software, while quantitative data sits in statistical packages, databases, or scripting environments such as Python or R. Combining them often requires a shared project structure that links coded text or annotations to numeric records, for example through case identifiers or timestamps. Cloud storage and version control help keep the two data streams aligned during analysis.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: A common pattern is to collect both types of data in parallel or sequence, then integrate them at the design, analysis, or interpretation stage. Researchers may quantify qualitative codes to compare frequencies, or use qualitative case studies to explain outliers in a quantitative model. Another approach is to build a joint display or matrix that places quotes beside statistics for the same cases. The integration should be planned before data collection so that each data type can answer part of the research question.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Combining data types raises distinct rights and risk issues because qualitative material often contains identifiable personal detail while quantitative data may be aggregated or anonymized. Consent for one use does not automatically cover the other, and linking a quote to a numeric record can re-identify a person. Researchers need to track provenance for both streams, document how they were merged, and apply access controls that respect the most sensitive source. Review boards or data stewards typically expect a clear account of how integration affects privacy and reuse.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The practice is moving toward more systematic and reproducible mixed methods, with shared templates for joint displays and clearer reporting standards. As language models make it easier to code large volumes of text, researchers are exploring how automated coding can be checked against human judgment and then combined with quantitative results. The likely direction is not to replace human interpretation but to make the link between qualitative and quantitative evidence more transparent and auditable.
